Detect Path Anomalies via HYPA

Source: R/hypa.R
build_hypa.Rd

build_hypa() tests which paths in a set of sequences occur more or less often than expected, with HYPA (LaRock et al., 2020). For an order k it builds the order-k De Bruijn graph, whose nodes are runs of k states and whose edges are paths of k + 1 states, and compares each path's count with a hypergeometric null model that keeps every node's observed in- and out-strength. Paths that are rarer than the null model allows are labelled under-represented, paths that are more common over-represented, and the rest normal. Unobserved paths that the observed transitions make possible are tested too, so a path that never occurs can be under-represented. Several orders can be tested in one call.

A path is over-represented when its last state follows its k-state context more often than the null model predicts from the strengths of the De Bruijn nodes alone (at order 2, from the first-order transitions). Each path is tested on its own at alpha, so with many possible paths some are flagged by chance: p_adjust corrects for that, and with small counts the upper-tail test rejects more often than alpha (see p_adjust). Whether the sequences need a higher order overall is a separate question, tested by markov_order_test(); build_mogen() selects an order and build_hon() builds a network of variable order.

Usage

build_hypa(
  data,
  order = 2L,
  alpha = 0.05,
  min_count = 5L,
  p_adjust = "none",
  k = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'net_hypa'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_hypa'
summary(
  object,
  n = 10L,
  type = c("all", "over", "under"),
  order_by = c("sig", "freq", "frequency", "ratio", "path"),
  ...
)

Arguments

data

The sequences: a wide data frame (one row per trajectory, position columns only, named as a numbered run), a character matrix with the same layout, a list of character vectors, a tna model, or a netobject built from sequences. For a tna model or a netobject, numeric state codes are converted to their labels. A frame with other columns beside the positions, a frame or matrix of only 0 and 1, a netobject_group, and a one-hot or association network raise an error of class nestimate_bad_input.

order

The order or orders of the De Bruijn graph, whole numbers of at least 1 without duplicates. Default 2. Order k tests paths of k + 1 states (k transitions), each conditioned on the k-state context before its last state. With several orders, one layer is built per order, in ascending order whatever the order given; an order with no paths (longer than the sequences allow) is dropped without a message, and an error is raised when none is left. The network fields (weights, edges, adjacency, xi, nodes, meta) describe the lowest order built, while scores holds every order.

alpha

The significance threshold for the labels, a number in (0, 0.5). Default 0.05. A path is under-represented when its adjusted lower-tail p-value (p_adjusted_under) is below alpha, otherwise over-represented when its adjusted upper-tail p-value (p_adjusted_over) is at most alpha, and normal otherwise.

min_count

The smallest count a path needs to be labelled, a whole number of at least 1. Default 5. An over-represented path must be observed at least min_count times, an under-represented path expected at least min_count times under the null model, so a path that never occurs can still be under-represented. Paths below it are normal.

p_adjust

The correction of the p-values for multiple testing: any of stats::p.adjust.methods, such as "BH" for Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control. Default "none", which compares the raw p-values with alpha, as LaRock et al. (2020) do. Under- and over-representation p-values are adjusted separately, within each order, over every possible path. With small counts the paper's upper-tail score P(X > f) rejects more often than alpha under the null, so neither the raw nor the corrected labels carry an exact type-I error or false discovery rate guarantee; min_count limits the problem.

k

The former name of order, deprecated: when given, it replaces order, with a warning of class deprecatedWarning. Default NULL.

x

For the print() method: a net_hypa.

...

For the print() and summary() methods: ignored.

object

For the summary() method: a net_hypa.

n

For the summary() method: the most paths to show and return per direction. Default 10.

type

For the summary() method: which anomalies to show, "all" (default), "over" or "under".

order_by

For the summary() method: how the paths are ranked within each direction before the top n are kept. "sig" (default) ranks by the tail probability of that direction, "freq" (or "frequency") by observed count, "ratio" by observed / expected (highest first for over-represented paths, lowest first for under-represented ones), and "path" alphabetically. With type = "all" the returned rows of both directions are ranked together the same way, by how far the ratio is from 1 on the log scale (abs(log(ratio))) for "ratio".

Value

A net_hypa object (class c("net_hypa", "cograph_network")). print() reports the orders, the number of paths tested and how many are over- and under-represented (per order when there are several); summary() prints and returns the strongest anomalies; pathways() gives the anomalous paths as pathway strings for cograph::plot_simplicial(). The object's fields:

scores

A data frame with one row per possible path of each order: every observed path and every unobserved one the observed transitions permit (observed = 0). Within each order the over-represented paths come first (by decreasing ratio), then the under-represented (by increasing ratio), then the rest. Columns: path, the full state sequence ("A -> B -> C"); from, the context (the conditioning states); to, the next state; observed; expected, the count under the null model, whose propensity matrix keeps the observed in- and out-strength of every De Bruijn node (at order 2 this equals the first-order Markov expectation \(n(a b \cdot) n(\cdot b c) / n(\cdot b \cdot)\)); ratio, observed / expected; p_under, the hypergeometric lower-tail probability P(X <= observed), and p_value, the same value under its older name; p_over, the strict upper tail P(X > observed) = 1 - p_under, so that p_over <= alpha is the paper's HYPA score of at least 1 - alpha; p_adjusted_under and p_adjusted_over, the same after p_adjust; anomaly ("over", "under" or "normal"); and order.

ho_edges

The same table as scores, under the name the other higher-order builders use.

over, under

The rows of scores labelled over- or under-represented.

adjacency

The weighted adjacency matrix (path counts) of the lowest-order De Bruijn graph.

weights

The cograph weight matrix of the lowest-order graph.

xi

The fitted propensity matrix of the lowest-order graph.

edges

The cograph edge data frame of the lowest-order graph.

by_order

A list with the results of each order built, named by order.

order

The orders built, ascending.

k

The same as order, kept for backward compatibility.

alpha

The significance threshold used.

p_adjust

The correction used.

n_anomalous, n_over, n_under

The number of anomalous, over- and under-represented paths, over all orders.

n_edges

The number of possible paths tested, over all orders.

nodes

A data frame (id, label, name) of the nodes of the lowest-order De Bruijn graph; label and name are the node's k states joined by the internal separator "\x01", as are the dimnames of adjacency, weights and xi.

directed

Always TRUE.

meta

The cograph meta list of the lowest-order graph.

node_groups

Always NULL.

print() returns its input invisibly. summary() prints the settings, the anomaly counts and the top n paths of each direction, and returns invisibly a data frame of those paths, one row per path: order (the De Bruijn order the path was tested at), path, observed, expected, ratio, p_tail (the raw tail probability of its direction, p_over for over-represented paths and p_under for under-represented ones) and direction ("over" or "under"). When nothing is anomalous it is a zero-row data frame with the same columns except order.

Details

Internal missing states split a trajectory, so no path spans a gap, and pieces shorter than two states are dropped. State labels must not contain the control characters "\x01" or "\x02", which are used internally as separators; such labels raise an error of class nestimate_hypa_bad_label.

The possible paths of order k link each node with an observed outgoing path to every node with an observed incoming path that continues it (its last k - 1 states are the other's first) through an observed first-order transition; at order 1 they are the observed transitions. The propensity matrix of the null model is fitted on them by continuous iterative proportional fitting; when the fit does not reach its tolerance, a warning of class nestimate_hypa_no_converge is raised. The original Python implementation rounds the propensities inside every sweep, so its expected counts can differ from these by a few thousandths.

As in the original implementation, when an order has only one possible path, that path's upper-tail p-value is 0, so it is labelled over-represented once it is observed min_count times, even when its count equals the expected one.

References

LaRock, T., Nanumyan, V., Scholtes, I., Casiraghi, G., Eliassi-Rad, T., & Schweitzer, F. (2020). HYPA: Efficient Detection of Path Anomalies in Time Series Data on Networks. SDM 2020, 460-468.

Examples

seqs <- list(c("A","B","C"), c("B","C","A"), c("A","C","B"), c("A","B","C"))
hyp <- build_hypa(seqs, order = 2)

# \donttest{
trajs <- list(c("A","B","C"), c("A","B","C"), c("A","B","C"),
              c("A","B","D"), c("C","B","D"), c("C","B","A"))
h <- build_hypa(trajs, order = 2)
print(h)
#> HYPA: Path Anomaly Detection
#>   Order(s):     2
#>   Edges:        6
#>   Anomalous:    0 (alpha=0.05, p_adjust=none)
#>     Over-repr:  0
#>     Under-repr: 0
# }
